transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
After 23 years, US military forces are officially out of Iraq.
Today marks their formal departure.
In March of 2003, President George W. Bush launched Operation Iraqi Freedom,
arguing Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein possessed or was working to obtain weapons of mass destruction
in violation of UN resolutions.
It was later determined Iraq had no WMD stockpiles.
At the height of the war, the US had 170,000 soldiers and personnel in the country.
More than 4,000 American troops lost their lives in decades of war.
Tens of thousands more were injured.
President Trump's tariff policies will be the focus today when a specialized trade court holds a hearing.
As NPR Scott Horsley reports, two previous efforts by the president to tax nearly all US imports were found to be illegal.
Since July, President Trump has imposed double-digit tariffs on nearly all US imports
in what the administration claims as a response to forced labor.
But opponents say the administration made no effort to differentiate between goods from countries
where forced labor is common and those where it's not.
Critics say the forced labor claim is a mere pretext,
and the tariffs are really just a third attempt by the administration to impose worldwide tariffs
after two earlier rounds were struck down by the courts.
Several importers in nearly two dozen states are asking the Court of International Trade
to overturn these latest import taxes.
They also want the court to order the Trump administration to refund the money it's already collected.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
A man shot and wounded during an immigration enforcement effort in Texas this month
is now charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Moses Buchel with member station KUT says that shooting occurred during a traffic stop in Austin
and involved an officer with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
In early accounts from his legal team, Wilbur Garces Perez said he did not know he was being pursued
by immigration agents before he was shot.
But a criminal complaint filed by ICE says officers identified themselves during an initial stop
before he fled in his car, hitting one of them with a side-view mirror.
That led to a chase and ended with one agent forcing a stop, then shooting Garces Perez,
saying he feared he'd be struck by the car.
The criminal complaint says one of the two officers was wearing a body camera for the initial stop,
but that the agent turned the camera off before arriving at the scene of the shooting.
Garces Perez has filed a federal lawsuit, primarily seeking to block deportation.
I'm Moses Buchel in Austin.
Flooded roads are reported across much of New Mexico and areas of Arizona,
from the remnants of Hurricane Polo.
The National Weather Service has issued flood watches and warnings from Arizona to Central Texas,
northward to Iowa and South Dakota.
Heavy rains continue falling across a wide area.
Some water rescues have been reported.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Prosecutors in Massachusetts are still deciding whether Lindsay Clancy will be retried
on charges of killing her three young children.
Clancy appeared in court yesterday for the first time since a mistrial was declared in her case earlier this month.
Deborah Becker with member station WBUR reports.
Judge William Sullivan took several motions under advisement filed by both sides
and set another hearing date for November.
Some motions asked the judge to dismiss the case.
Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz said his office is still considering whether there will be a new trial.
No determination to me that's anything.
We're doing it.
We're doing it.
We're doing a due diligence.
We're going to continue to do that.
Cruz did not say when he would decide
or whether Clancy would be charged with first-degree murder again or lesser charges.
For NPR News, I'm Deborah Becker in Boston.
It's been two centuries since the state of Tennessee has executed a woman.
This morning, a woman convicted of a 1995 murder is scheduled to be put to death by lethal injection at a maximum security prison.
Fifty-year-old Christa Gail Pike was convicted, along with her boyfriend,
of fatally stabbing a 19-year-old woman at a job training facility in Knoxville.
The victim was a classmate of Pike's.
Her supporters have cited Pike's history of mental illness and severe sexual abuse as a child.
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to halt the execution. Tennessee's governor denied clemency.
Later this morning, ADP will release its report on the number of jobs
added by private employers in the U.S. for the month of September.
I'm Dave Mattingly in Washington.
Thanks for watching.
Please subscribe to our channel and follow us on social media.

topics.text: US military forces officially depart Iraq after 23 years, ending Operation Iraqi Freedom
Trump tariff policies on nearly all US imports face specialized trade court hearing today
Man shot by ICE officer during Texas traffic stop now charged with assaulting federal officer
Flooded roads reported across New Mexico and Arizona from remnants of Hurricane Polo
Massachusetts prosecutors still deciding whether to retry Lindsay Clancy on charges of killing three children
Tennessee scheduled to execute Christa Gail Pike this morning, first woman execution in two centuries
